add-the-squares.title: Add the Squares
add-the-squares.closing: Variances add, standard deviations do not. Square them, add them, and take the root at the end, and any coefficient gets squared on the way through.

brief.title: Variances add, spreads do not
steps: Two uncertain loads on one beam
One load wobbles by about 3 kN, the other by about 8 kN. How much does their total wobble? Not 11. The two rarely wobble the same way at the same moment.
Draw them as a right triangle
Put 3 along one leg and 8 up the other. The total spread is the slanted side, and a slanted side is always shorter than walking round the two legs. Here it is 8.54.
So square, add, then root
Variances add: 9 plus 64 is 73. The spread is the square root, 8.54. Standard deviations never add on their own. Any number multiplying a variable gets squared on the way in.
Means just add
The average of a total is the totals of the averages, always, even when the two are not independent. Only the variances need independence to add.
spoken: means add straight, with their multipliers
variances add, and each multiplier is squared
square each spread, add, take the root

picture.caption: two spreads as the legs of a triangle. The total is the slanted side, not 3 plus 8

rounds.why: Eleven is the two legs laid end to end, and the triangle says plainly that the direct route is shorter. Seventy three is the variance, which is the number you get one step before the square root.

screen.text: What is the standard deviation of the total load?

screen.mono: dead load and live load on a bridge beam

rounds.why: Six and eight give ten, which is a triangle everyone has met. Adding them gives fourteen, and fourteen millimeters would be a longer straight line than the two legs can reach.

screen.text: What is the standard deviation of the combined error?

screen.mono: two independent survey measurements

rounds.why: Five and twelve give thirteen. Seventeen is the sum, and it is the answer that would be right only if the two segments always ran long together, which is what independent means they do not.

screen.text: What is the standard deviation of the total travel time?

screen.mono: travel time on two independent segments

rounds.why: Variances add, so this one is a plain sum: nine and sixty four. The square root is what turns it back into a standard deviation, and this question did not ask for one.

screen.text: What is the VARIANCE of the total load?

screen.mono: the same dead and live loads

rounds.why: The small spread barely moves the answer: nine becomes nine point two. Squaring makes the big one dominate, which is why tightening the already-tight measurement buys you almost nothing.

screen.text: What is the standard deviation of the total?

screen.mono: a precise gauge alongside a rough one

rounds.why: The coefficient gets squared along with the standard deviation, which is the same as saying it doubles the leg before the triangle is drawn. Eleven is what you get by forgetting the two entirely.

screen.text: What is the standard deviation of the total?

screen.mono: a load counted twice, plus an independent one

how-do-they-sit.title: How Do They Sit
how-do-they-sit.closing: Two questions, asked in this order. Could both happen at once? If not they are exclusive and their probabilities simply add. If so, does the first change the odds of the second? If not you may multiply them straight out, and if so you need the conditional. Exclusive and independent are not two words for one idea. They are opposites.

brief.title: Two questions before either rule
steps: Can both happen at once
If two things can never happen together, like a coin landing heads and tails, their circles do not overlap. The chance of one OR the other is just the two chances added.
If they can, take the overlap off
If both can happen, like rain and wind, the circles overlap. Adding the two chances counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once.
Does the first change the second

For the chance of one AND the other, ask whether the first happening changes the odds of the second. If not, they are independent: multiply the two chances. If it does, multiply by the chance of the second GIVEN the first.
Exclusive is not independent
Drawing cards without putting them back quietly makes events dependent. And events that cannot both happen are as dependent as they come: one of them drops the other to zero.
spoken: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
A or B: add them, take the overlap off once
A and B: the chance of A, times the chance of B given A
A changes nothing, so just multiply

left.caption: cannot both happen: nothing shared, just add

right.caption: can both happen: the middle got counted twice

options: One does not affect the other
One changes the odds of the other
rounds.why: They cannot both happen. One die, one roll, one face upward, so there is no overlap and nothing to subtract: the chance of a 3 or a 5 is simply one sixth plus one sixth. Note what this is NOT. These two are about as far from independent as events get, because a 3 drops the chance of a 5 straight to zero.

screen.mono: one roll of one die

c.v: mutually exclusive, so nothing to subtract

independent, so the two just multiply

Almost the same sentence as the round before, and a different world: there the two faces were competing for one die, here they have one each.

how-many-samples.title: How Many Samples
how-many-samples.closing: The margin falls with the root of n, so halving it costs four times the samples and a third of it costs nine times. And the answer always rounds UP: a sample size that misses the spec is not a sample size.

brief.title: Working backwards to how many samples
steps: Fix the margin first
Sometimes the margin is decided before any data: the count has to be good to within 200 vehicles. The question becomes how many days to count.
Turn the margin formula around

The margin is the multiplier times sigma over root n. Solve for n: multiplier times sigma over the margin, and then SQUARE the whole thing. Stop before the square and you get about 8 when the answer is 62.
The square is why halving costs four times
Cut the margin in half and n goes up by four. The curve of margin against samples drops fast at first and then flattens out.
Round up, always
The arithmetic gives 61.47. Sixty-one days misses the target, and there is no such thing as most of a day. Take 62.
spoken: multiplier times sigma, over the margin, then squared
the ratio is 7.84, and squared it is 61.47

picture.caption: margin against sample count. The curve crosses the target between 61 and 62, so 62

rounds.why: The formula gives 61.47, and 61 days leaves the margin just above the line. You cannot count for half a day, and you cannot round down to a number that misses the spec, so it is 62.

screen.text: The margin has to be 200 vehicles. How many days do you count?

screen.mono: daily traffic counts at an intersection

rounds.why: Halving the margin costs four times the samples, because the margin falls with the ROOT of n. Doubling to fifty gets you to about 2.8, which is most of the effort and none of the answer.

screen.text: 25 samples give a margin of 4. How many give a margin of 2?

screen.mono: liquid limit on soil samples

rounds.why: A third of the margin costs nine times the samples. This is the number that ends conversations about tightening a spec, and it is worth being able to produce before the meeting rather than after.

screen.text: 36 counts give a margin of 6. How many give a margin of 2?

screen.mono: a survey being retendered to a tighter spec

rounds.why: The formula gives 15.37. Fifteen is not enough and sixteen is, and twenty is paying for precision the specification never asked for.

screen.text: The margin has to be 50 psi. How many cylinders?

screen.mono: compressive strength on a small pour

rounds.why: It runs the other way too. Letting the margin double lets the sample size drop to a quarter, which is the cheapest saving on the sheet and the first thing worth asking a client about.

screen.text: 64 samples give a margin of 5. How many give a margin of 10?

screen.mono: a spec that has just been relaxed

rounds.why: Sigma sits inside the square, so doubling it costs four times the samples to stand still. Everything in this formula that doubles on the top costs a factor of four on the bottom.

screen.text: 30 samples were planned on sigma = 400. Sigma is really 800, and the margin must hold. How many samples?

screen.mono: a material that turns out to vary more than assumed

r-or-r2.title: Which One Do They Want
r-or-r2.closing: Correlation is r and carries a sign. Determination is r squared, is always positive, and is the share of the variation explained. The exam asks for them in English, so the reading is the work.

brief.title: Correlation, or determination
steps: Two numbers from one cloud
r is the correlation: which way the cloud leans and how tightly. r squared is the coefficient of determination: the share of the ups and downs in y that x accounts for.
Squaring drops the sign
r can be negative; r squared never is. An r of minus 0.92 means a tight downward lean, and an r squared of 0.85 means x explains 85 percent of what y does. The other 15 percent is something else.
Hear which one was asked

The exam asks in English. "Correlation" wants r, with its sign. "Coefficient of determination" or "share explained" wants r squared. A negative coefficient of determination is not wrong, it is impossible.
spoken: minus 0.92 squared is 0.85, and the minus is gone

picture.caption: r is minus 0.92. Squared, 0.85 of the variation is explained and 0.15 is not

rounds.why: Variation explained is r squared, and squaring throws the sign away. Ninety two percent is the correlation itself, which answers a question nobody asked.

screen.text: What percentage of the variation in condition rating is explained by the age of the bridge?

v.done: one take the size of r

rounds.why: Asked for r, hand back r, minus sign and all. The sign is half of what it tells you: rating falls as age rises.

screen.text: What is the correlation coefficient?

v.done: the size of r, sign dropped

rounds.why: A correlation of zero point seven sounds strong and explains under half. Squaring is unkind to middling correlations, which is exactly why the exam asks for the squared one.

screen.text: How much of the variation does the regression account for?

rounds.why: Going back the other way, the square root gives the size and the question gives the sign. R squared has already thrown the direction away, so it has to be told to you or read off the plot.

screen.text: What is the correlation coefficient?

v.done: the root, with the sign put back

rounds.why: A quarter is explained, so three quarters is not. The unexplained share is what is left over from r squared, never from r.

screen.text: What fraction of the variation is NOT explained by the regression?

rounds.why: Determination is always positive, because it is a share of something and a share cannot be less than none. A minus sign on an R squared is a wrong answer you can spot without doing any arithmetic.

screen.text: What is the coefficient of determination?

v.done: the root of the size of r

read-the-scatter.title: Read the Scatter
read-the-scatter.closing: The lean gives the sign and the tightness gives the size. And r only ever measures how well a STRAIGHT line fits, so a cloud can have an obvious shape and a correlation of nothing.

brief.title: What r is telling you
steps: Look at the cloud
Plot pairs of readings as dots. If the dots rise together they lean one way; if one goes up while the other goes down they lean the other. If they hug a straight line, the cloud is tight.
r is that lean and that tightness
r runs from minus one to plus one. Its sign is the direction of the lean. Its size is how tightly the dots hug a line: near one is tight, near zero is a shapeless cloud.
Only straight lines

r only measures agreement with a STRAIGHT line. A cloud that rises and then falls has an obvious shape and an r of about nothing. So r near zero does not mean no relationship. It means no straight one.
spoken: from minus one, a perfect fall, to plus one, a perfect rise
A perfect rise, and a perfect fall
every dot exactly on one straight line
either a shapeless cloud, or a shape that is not straight

left.caption: tight and rising: r near plus one

right.caption: loose and falling: r about minus a half

children.caption: and this one has r of exactly zero. There is plainly a pattern, it is just not a straight one. r near zero means no straight line, not no relationship

rounds.why: Up and to the right, and hugging a line all the way. More rain, more runoff, and very little scatter about it, so r sits just under one.

screen.text: Which correlation is this closest to?

screen.mono: rainfall depth against runoff volume

rounds.why: Down and to the right, and just as tight. The minus sign is the direction and nothing else; a correlation of minus one is exactly as strong as one of plus one.

screen.text: Which correlation is this closest to?

screen.mono: bridge age against condition rating

rounds.why: It leans up, but loosely. Around zero point seven, which squares to about half, so a line through this would explain only half of what the readings do.

screen.text: Which correlation is this closest to?

screen.mono: blow count against shear strength

rounds.why: No lean at all. Knowing x tells you nothing about y here, and a regression line through this cloud would predict about as well as guessing the average every time.

screen.text: Which correlation is this closest to?

screen.mono: two site measurements with nothing between them

rounds.why: Every reading is exactly on one line, so r is one on the nose. This is as good as it gets and it almost never happens with field data.

screen.text: Which correlation is this closest to?

screen.mono: a gauge reading against the quantity it measures

rounds.why: There is obviously a relationship here, and r is still zero. It only measures STRAIGHT-line agreement, and this arch rises and falls by the same amount, so the two halves cancel. An r of nothing never means there is nothing going on.

screen.text: Which correlation is this closest to?

screen.mono: compaction moisture against dry density

reject-or-not.title: Reject or Not
reject-or-not.closing: Bigger than the critical value means reject, for z, for t and for chi-square alike. And failing to reject is never a finding: it says the data did not catch the null out, not that the null is true.

brief.title: Bigger means reject
steps: One number against one line
Work one number out of your data. Look one number up in a table. Put both on the same scale. If your number lands past the line, the boring claim is rejected. That is the whole test.
What the two numbers are

Yours says how far the sample strayed from the claim. The table one is the line drawn where straying that far stops being believable. It is called the critical value, and it is chosen before you look.
With no direction, size is all that counts
When the claim did not say which way, only the distance from zero matters. Minus 2.9 against a line at 2.131 is past it, because 2.9 is further from zero. It rejects.
Staying short of the line proves nothing
It means the data did not catch the boring claim out. That is all. An answer saying the mean really does equal the claimed value is wrong, however right the decision beside it looks.
spoken: how far the sample mean sits from the claim, in standard errors
the same, with s from the sample, on n minus one degrees of freedom

picture.caption: the statistic and the critical value on one line. Past the line means reject

options: Reject H0. There is evidence the mean exceeds 200 kPa.
Fail to reject H0. Not enough evidence that it exceeds 200 kPa.
Reject H0. The mean is proven to be above 200 kPa.
rounds.why: Bigger than the critical value, so reject. Evidence FOR a claim is not proof of it, and an exam choice that says proven is wrong however right the decision beside it is.

screen.text: What is the correct conclusion?

screen.mono: bearing capacity claimed to exceed 200 kPa
t = 2.4 against t(0.05, 15) = 1.753, one-tailed right

child.v: Reject H0. There is evidence the mean exceeds 200 kPa.
Fail to reject H0. Not enough evidence that it exceeds 200 kPa.
Reject H0. The mean is proven to be above 200 kPa.

Reject. The uniform model does not fit.
Fail to reject. The uniform model is not contradicted by this data.
rounds.why: Five is under the line, so there is nothing to reject. That is not the same as the arrivals being uniform: two hundred observations failed to catch it out, and that is all.

screen.mono: uniform arrivals across four periods
chi-square = 5.0 against 7.815 at three degrees of freedom

Reject. The uniform model does not fit.
Fail to reject. The uniform model is not contradicted by this data.

options: Fail to reject. Two and 1.96 are near enough the same.
Reject H0. The mean differs from 4,000 psi.
Reject H0. The mean is above 4,000 psi.
rounds.why: Past the line is past the line, by however little. And the test was two-tailed, so what it supports is that the mean DIFFERS, not which way it went.

screen.mono: a mix tested against 4,000 psi in both directions
z = 2.0 against 1.960, two-tailed at alpha = 0.05

Reject H0. The mean is above 4,000 psi.

options: Reject H0. The sample mean came out above the specified value.
Fail to reject H0. Not enough evidence at this level.
Fail to reject H0. The mean equals the specified value.
rounds.why: The sample mean being on the right side of the specification is not the test; the test is whether it is far enough over to be surprising, and 1.2 is not.

Fail to reject H0. Not enough evidence at this level.
Fail to reject H0. The mean equals the specified value.

options: Fail to reject. A bigger chi-square means the fit is better.
Reject. The counts do not match the uniform model.
Reject. The counts match the uniform model badly enough to be certain.
rounds.why: Chi-square measures MISFIT, so bigger is worse and past the line means reject. Certainty is not on offer either: this is a five percent test and it can be wrong five times in a hundred.

chi-square = 12.4 against 7.815 at three degrees of freedom

Reject. The counts do not match the uniform model.

options: Reject H0. The mean thickness differs from the target.
Fail to reject. The statistic is negative and the critical value is not.
Reject H0. The mean thickness is exactly 2.131 below the target.
rounds.why: A two-tailed test compares SIZE. Minus 2.9 is further out than 2.131 and lands in the left rejection region, which the picture makes obvious and the algebra hides behind an absolute value.

same-pick.title: Same Pick, or Not
same-pick.closing: Nothing about the names decides it. Ask whether the scenario counts the same picks in another order as a second result: if it does, order matters and it is nPr, and if it does not, it is nCr.

brief.title: Does the order count, or just the group
steps: Pick three from a pool
Say three letters from A, B and C. You could pick them as ABC, or ACB, or BAC, and so on. Six ways. But every one of those is the same three letters.
When order matters
If the first pick gets a different job from the second, a rank, a position, a place in a sequence, then ABC and BAC are different results. That count is a permutation, and it is the bigger number.
When it does not

If all three picks get treated the same, the six orderings are one group. That count is a combination. It is the permutation count divided by the number of ways to order the picks, which is r factorial.
spoken: n factorial over the factorial of what is left
the same, divided once more by r factorial
three picks can be ordered six ways, so divide by six

picture.caption: pick three letters. Six orderings, but only one group if order does not matter

rounds.why: A team is a team. Writing the same three names in another order does not make a second team, so the two lists are one result and this is a combination.

screen.text: Three of eight qualified engineers are chosen to form ONE inspection team for a bridge deck pour.

rounds.why: The same three names, and now the position is a job. Alvarez on the deck is a different assignment from Alvarez on the abutments, so these are two results and the count is six times bigger.

screen.text: Three of the same eight engineers are assigned, one each, to the deck, the girders and the abutments.

rounds.why: The lab receives four samples. Which one was written down first is a fact about the paperwork, not about the selection.

screen.text: Four of twelve boreholes are selected for laboratory testing.

rounds.why: Ranking is order made explicit. The same three firms in another order is a different award, and a contractor who came second would tell you so.

screen.text: The three lowest bids are ranked first, second and third for award.

rounds.why: Both mixes get batched. There is no first and no second, only the pair, so the two lists are the same pair written twice.

screen.text: Two of six trial mixes are chosen to be batched and tested together.

rounds.why: A sequence is nothing but an order. Swapping the first two lifts is a different schedule, and here every lift is used, which is why this one is a plain factorial.

screen.text: The four lifts of a pour are sequenced, and the schedule says which goes down first.

which-cell-hurts.title: Which Cell Hurts Most
which-cell-hurts.closing: Each cell contributes the gap SQUARED and then divided by what was expected. That division is why a small category with a small gap can outweigh a large one with a large gap, and why the biggest bar on the chart is often not the culprit.

brief.title: Every cell pays its own way
steps: Do the counts match the model
A model says each of four patterns should show up 50 times. You counted 62, 45, 53 and 40. Chi-square asks whether those gaps are bigger than chance would give.
Each cell adds its own piece
For every category: the gap between counted and expected, squared, then divided by what was expected. Add the pieces up. Bigger means a worse fit.
The division is the point

A gap of ten where a hundred was expected is a small surprise. A gap of eight where twenty was expected is a big one. Dividing by the expectation is what tells them apart, and it is the step the exam watches for.
Degrees of freedom
One less than the number of categories. Look the critical value up on that row and apply the same rule as always: bigger means reject.
spoken: for each cell, the gap squared over what was expected, all added
the number of categories, less one
the smaller gap hurts more, because less was expected

picture.caption: what was counted as bars, what was expected as a line. The biggest gap pays the most

rounds.why: Every category expected the same fifty, so with a level model the biggest gap wins outright. Twelve over beats ten under once both are squared.

screen.text: Which category contributes most to the chi-square total?

screen.mono: 200 arrivals spread evenly, so 50 expected in each
the bar is what was counted, the line is what was expected

rounds.why: Beam is eighteen out and Deck only sixteen, and Deck still hurts more because less was expected of it. The division by E is what makes chi-square a comparison rather than a tally of gaps.

screen.text: Which category contributes most to the chi-square total?

screen.mono: a maintenance model predicting 100, 60, 20 and 20
the bar is what was counted, the line is what was expected

rounds.why: Friday is thirty over and Thursday twenty five under, and the squaring pulls them apart further than the raw gaps suggest. A category sitting exactly on its expectation adds nothing at all.

screen.text: Which category contributes most to the chi-square total?

screen.mono: 200 inspections across five days, so 40 expected each
the bar is what was counted, the line is what was expected

rounds.why: Grade B is ten out and grade A only eight, and A still wins. Twenty expected against eighty is the whole difference, and it is the reason small categories drive chi-square.

screen.text: Which category contributes most to the chi-square total?

screen.mono: a quality model predicting 20, 80, 80 and 20
the bar is what was counted, the line is what was expected

rounds.why: Clay is eighteen out and Sand only twelve, and Sand is the bigger problem. Reading the biggest gap off the chart and stopping there is the mistake this round exists for.

screen.text: Which category contributes most to the chi-square total?

screen.mono: a site model predicting 120, 40 and 40
the bar is what was counted, the line is what was expected

rounds.why: Q1 lands exactly on the model and contributes nothing, which is what a perfect cell looks like. Q2 carries most of the statistic on its own, and two equal cells behind it share the rest.

screen.text: Which category contributes most to the chi-square total?

screen.mono: 200 complaints spread evenly, so 50 expected in each
the bar is what was counted, the line is what was expected

wider-or-narrower.title: Wider or Narrower
wider-or-narrower.closing: Three things set the width: how sure you want to be, how spread out the material is, and how many samples you took. The sample mean is not one of them, and t is always wider than z.

brief.title: Sigma or s, and which way the width moves
steps: Where did the spread come from
If the problem hands you sigma, the spread of the whole population, use the z multiplier. If it hands you s, a spread you worked out from your own few samples, use t.
t is always wider

With s, the spread itself is a guess, and the interval has to pay for that. So t at the same confidence is a bigger multiplier than z, and the difference shrinks as you take more samples. t uses n minus one degrees of freedom.
What moves the width
Three things: the confidence you ask for, the spread, and how many samples. The sample mean is not one of them. It slides the interval along; it does not stretch it.
spoken: the same shape, with t for z and s for sigma, on n minus one degrees of freedom
the t multiplier is bigger, so the interval is wider

picture.caption: ten samples at 95 percent. The t interval is wider because the spread is a guess too

ops.t: t: s came from the sample

rounds.why: Four times the samples halve the margin, because the root of four is two. That is the whole economics of sampling: the interval improves with the root of the effort, never with the effort.

screen.overline: WHICH WAY DOES THE INTERVAL MOVE

screen.text: You go back and collect 100 samples instead of 25.

screen.mono: 25 samples, sigma known, reported at 95%

rounds.why: Being surer costs width. The multiplier goes from 1.960 to 2.576 and the interval grows by about a third, which is the price of the extra four percent of confidence.

screen.overline: WHICH WAY DOES THE INTERVAL MOVE

screen.text: The report is reissued at 99% confidence instead of 95%.

screen.mono: 25 samples, sigma known, reported at 95%

rounds.why: The t interval is always the wider one at the same confidence, because the spread is now a guess too and the interval has to pay for that. With ten samples the multiplier goes from 1.960 to 2.262.

screen.overline: WHICH WAY DOES THE INTERVAL MOVE

screen.text: Sigma was never actually known. You have s from the sample, so you switch to t with nine degrees of freedom.

screen.mono: 10 cylinders, 95% confidence

rounds.why: The interval slides up the axis and keeps its width. Nothing in the margin formula mentions the mean, and noticing that is worth more than memorising the formula.

screen.overline: WHICH WAY DOES THE INTERVAL MOVE

screen.text: The cylinders come back stronger than expected, so the sample mean is higher. Everything else is unchanged.

screen.mono: 10 cylinders, s known, 95% confidence

rounds.why: Half the spread, half the margin, and this one is a straight halving rather than a root. Consistency is the cheapest way to a tight interval, which is why specifications chase it.

screen.overline: WHICH WAY DOES THE INTERVAL MOVE

screen.text: The material turns out to be more consistent: sigma is really 2.5.

screen.mono: 25 samples, sigma assumed to be 5, reported at 95%

rounds.why: It helps, and barely. Twenty one more days of counting buys nine percent off the margin, which is the flat end of the curve and the reason sample size is planned before the counting starts.

screen.overline: WHICH WAY DOES THE INTERVAL MOVE

screen.text: The budget stretches to 121 samples rather than 100.

screen.mono: 100 samples already counted, reported at 95%

which-way-points.title: Which Way Does It Point
which-way-points.closing: The claim decides the picture. A directional word puts all of alpha in one tail, and no direction splits it between two, which is a different row of the table and a different critical value.

brief.title: Which way the claim points
steps: Two rival statements
The null is the boring one: nothing has changed, the mean is what it always was. The alternative is what somebody is trying to show. The test assumes the null until the data makes it uncomfortable.
Read the claim for a direction
Words like exceeds, reduces or falls short point one way. Then the whole of alpha, the risk you accept of a false alarm, sits in ONE tail of the curve.
No direction, two tails
A claim like "is different from" could be wrong either way. Alpha gets split in half, one piece in each tail. That is a different row of the table and a bigger critical value.
The two ways to be wrong
Rejecting a null that was true is a Type I error, and alpha is its chance. Keeping a null that was false is a Type II error.
spoken: the claim points one way, so alpha sits in one tail
the claim could go either way, so alpha is split

children.caption: "falls short": all of alpha on the left
"exceeds": all of alpha on the right

rounds.why: Exceeds points one way. Only a sample mean far ABOVE 200 is evidence for the claim, so the whole of alpha sits in the right tail and the critical value comes from the one-tailed row.

screen.text: The engineer claims the mean bearing capacity EXCEEDS 200 kPa.

screen.mono: bearing capacity of a clay deposit

rounds.why: A minimum spec is only ever failed downwards. A batch that comes back stronger than 4,000 is not evidence of anything wrong, so the whole of alpha sits on the left.

screen.text: The spec sets a minimum of 4,000 psi. You are testing whether the mix FALLS SHORT of it.

screen.mono: compressive strength against a specified minimum

rounds.why: Both directions are failures, so both tails are rejection regions and alpha is split between them. Five percent overall means two and a half percent at each end, which is a different row of the table.

screen.text: The lift is specified at 2.00 in. Too thin fails the structure and too thick wastes material, so ANY deviation matters.

screen.mono: lift thickness against a target

rounds.why: Reduce is a direction. Delay coming out higher than before is not evidence that the retiming worked, however surprising it is, so there is nothing to reject on the right.

screen.text: The new timing plan is claimed to REDUCE the mean delay.

screen.mono: delay at a retimed signal

screen.code: H0: mu >= 42 s      H1: mu < 42 s

rounds.why: The supplier is making a directional claim and carrying the burden of proof for it. Everything that is not strong enough, however weak, leaves the claim unproven rather than disproven.

screen.text: The supplier claims the new mix is STRONGER than the standard mix.

screen.mono: a new mix against the standard one

rounds.why: No direction in the sentence means no direction in the test. Choosing a tail after seeing which way the data went is how a five percent test quietly becomes a ten percent one.

screen.text: Nobody has a direction in mind. The question is only whether the population mean is STILL 4,000 psi.

screen.mono: a routine check with nothing being claimed

through-the-means.title: Through the Means
through-the-means.closing: The least-squares line always passes through the point where the two means meet. That is where the intercept comes from, and it is why a prediction is the intercept plus the slope times x and never the slope alone.

brief.title: The best line goes through the means
steps: Draw the best straight line
Through a cloud of dots you can draw one straight line that misses them all by the least. That is the regression line, and it lets you predict y from an x you never measured.
It always passes through one point
Take the mean of all the x values and the mean of all the y values. Put a dot there. The best line goes through that dot, every time.
That is where the intercept comes from
A line is a slope plus a starting height. Knowing the slope and one point on the line gives you the starting height: the mean of y, less the slope times the mean of x.
Slope alone is not a prediction
Slope times x with nothing added is a line through the origin. It leans the right way in the wrong place. A prediction needs both parts.
spoken: a starting height, plus the slope times x
the mean of y, less the slope times the mean of x
b = \frac{n\sum x_i y_i - \sum x_i \sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}
sums from the data. The calculator does this one

picture.caption: the same slope twice. Only the line through the point of the means fits

rounds.why: B is the only one through the means. A has the right lean and starts at zero, which is the same mistake as predicting with the slope and forgetting the intercept, and it sits under every reading on the right of the plot.

screen.overline: IT HAS TO GO THROUGH THE MEANS

screen.text: Which of these could be the regression line?

screen.mono: rainfall against runoff

rounds.why: A is flat at the mean of y, which is what answering with the average every time looks like: it passes through the means and predicts the same thing for every blow count. A regression line has to lean AND go through the means.

screen.overline: IT HAS TO GO THROUGH THE MEANS

screen.text: Which of these could be the regression line?

screen.mono: blow count against shear strength

rounds.why: A. A falling line is no different: the rule is about the means, not about the sign of the slope. C starts in the right place and does not fall fast enough to reach the cloud on the right.

screen.overline: IT HAS TO GO THROUGH THE MEANS

screen.text: Which of these could be the regression line?

screen.mono: age against condition rating

rounds.why: Here the intercept really is zero, so the line through the origin is also the line through the means. The intercept is whatever the means and the slope make it, and sometimes that is nothing.

screen.overline: IT HAS TO GO THROUGH THE MEANS

screen.text: Which of these could be the regression line?

screen.mono: a tight pair of measurements

rounds.why: Same shape as the round before with everything lifted, and now the intercept carries that lift. A is the identical slope through the origin and misses every point, which is the cost of dropping the intercept term.

screen.overline: IT HAS TO GO THROUGH THE MEANS

screen.text: Which of these could be the regression line?

screen.mono: the same readings, offset

rounds.why: A, and it goes through the means even though it is nowhere near most of the readings. The rule holds however loose the cloud is; how well the line fits is what r is for, and it is a separate question.

screen.overline: IT HAS TO GO THROUGH THE MEANS

screen.text: Which of these could be the regression line?

screen.mono: a loose cloud that still leans

where-it-balances.title: Where It Balances
where-it-balances.closing: An expected value is the balance point of the whole picture. It is not the most likely outcome, it is not the middle of the range, and it does not have to be a value that can actually happen.

brief.title: A balance point, not a favorite
steps: Load the outcomes onto a beam
Each possible outcome is a block placed at its value. How likely it is sets how heavy the block is. Now find where a fulcrum would hold the beam level.
That point is the expected value
It is an average where the weights are the probabilities. Multiply each outcome by its chance and add. Over many repeats, that is what you get per go.
The two usual mistakes tip the beam
The most likely outcome is the tallest block, not the balance point: a heavy block further out still wins. And the plain middle of the range throws the weights away entirely.
It may be a value that never happens
A balance point can sit between blocks. An expected 8.4 trucks is a fine answer even though no day ever has 8.4 trucks.
spoken: each outcome times its chance, all added up
three outcomes, three chances, one balance point

picture.caption: outcomes as blocks, probabilities as their weight. The beam sits level at 8.4

rounds.why: Most of the weight is out at ten, so the balance point sits well to the right of the middle. It does not reach ten, though: the lighter blocks on the left still pull, and every one of them counts.

screen.text: Each block is an outcome, and its height is how likely it is.

screen.mono: trucks arriving per minute at a toll plaza

rounds.why: Five is the most likely single outcome and it is not the balance point. Nearly as much weight sits at one, and the pair of them together pull the fulcrum well to the left of the tallest block.

screen.text: Each block is an outcome, and its height is how likely it is.

screen.mono: lanes closed during a night shift

rounds.why: Six is the plain average of two, six and ten, which is the answer you get by ignoring the probabilities entirely. Sixty percent of the weight is down at two, and the beam knows it.

screen.text: Each block is an outcome, and its height is how likely it is.

screen.mono: days of delay on a utility relocation

rounds.why: Two equal weights balance halfway between them, and there is no block at five at all. An expected value is a long-run average, and it is under no obligation to be an outcome that can happen.

screen.text: Each block is an outcome, and its height is how likely it is.

screen.mono: a coin-flip choice between two repair strategies

rounds.why: Here the tallest block IS the balance point, because the picture is symmetric about it. That is exactly why reaching for the most likely outcome works often enough to feel like a rule.

screen.text: Each block is an outcome, and its height is how likely it is.

screen.mono: cylinders below strength in a day of testing

rounds.why: One rare, distant outcome drags the balance point off the crowd, but only as far as its weight can carry it. Ten percent out at eleven moves the fulcrum a little; it does not move it to the middle.

screen.text: Each block is an outcome, and its height is how likely it is.

screen.mono: claims filed against a contract, in hundreds of thousands

what-goes-under.title: What Goes Under
what-goes-under.closing: The margin is the multiplier times sigma over the ROOT of n. The root is what makes samples expensive, and the multiplier is what makes confidence expensive. Both show up as width.

brief.title: What sets the width of the interval
steps: A guess with a margin
You measured 25 samples and got a mean of 42. The true mean is probably near 42, but not exactly. A confidence interval is 42 plus or minus a margin, wide enough to catch the truth most of the time.
The margin has three parts
A multiplier for how sure you want to be. The spread of the readings, sigma. And the ROOT of how many you took. More samples narrow it, but slowly: four times the samples for half the width.
The root is the part people drop
Divide by n instead of the root of n and the interval collapses to a sliver. It claims a precision 25 samples cannot buy. If your margin looks tiny, check the root.
spoken: the sample mean, plus or minus the multiplier times sigma over root n
surer means a bigger multiplier and a wider interval
25 samples, root 5, a margin of about 2

picture.caption: the same 25 samples. Dropping the root shrinks the interval to a sliver it has not earned

rounds.why: The root of twenty five is five, so the standard error is one and the margin is about two. Dividing by twenty five instead gives an interval a fifth of a percent wide, which no soil lab has ever reported.

screen.mono: liquid limit on 25 soil samples

rounds.why: Ninety five percent is the one worth knowing by heart, and the other two are in the handbook. More confidence costs width: every one of these is a real answer to a differently worded question.

screen.mono: the same soil samples, reported at three confidence levels

rounds.why: Three and nine are close enough that the wrong one looks plausible on paper. On the picture it is the difference between an interval you would report and one that claims more precision than nine cylinders can buy.

screen.mono: compressive strength on 9 cylinders

rounds.why: Ninety nine percent is the widest of the three, because being surer means claiming less. Reaching for 1.960 out of habit reports an interval narrower than the confidence level it is labeled with.

screen.mono: a survey reported at 99% confidence

rounds.why: Four samples buy a factor of two, not a factor of four. That is the whole reason the root is there: the interval improves with the root of the effort, not with the effort.

screen.mono: a small set of 4 field tests

rounds.why: Ninety percent is the narrowest of the three, and it is narrow because it is admitting a bigger chance of being wrong. Width and confidence move together, always.

screen.mono: a routine check reported at 90% confidence

shade-the-tail.title: Shade the Tail
shade-the-tail.closing: The z-score is arithmetic and it belongs on paper. Which area the sentence wants is the part that gets marked wrong: left of the line, right of it, between two lines, or everything outside them.

brief.title: Which piece of the curve was asked for
steps: Turn the number into a z

A normal curve is a bell. Any bell can be turned into the one the handbook has a table for: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. That is the z-score, how many spreads from the middle you are.
The table has three columns
F is everything to the left of your cut. R is everything to the right. W is the band between minus z and plus z. Pick the column that matches the piece you shaded.
Negative z: flip it
The table only runs on positive z. The area left of a negative cut is one minus the area left of the same positive cut, because the bell is symmetric.
Fail rate and pass rate are the same line
How many fall below 4,000 psi and how many pass are the two halves of one picture. Decide which piece the sentence asked for before you open the table.
spoken: the value less the mean, over the standard deviation
the area left of minus z is one minus the area left of z
right of the cut is one minus left of it

children.caption: F: everything to the LEFT of the cut, here the fail rate
R: everything to the RIGHT of it, here the pass rate. F and R together make one
W: the band in the middle, the same distance either side

rounds.why: Failing means weaker than the spec, so it is everything to the LEFT of the line. The table gives the area left of a POSITIVE z, so this one comes from the flip: one take F of 1.67.

screen.overline: PUT A FINGER ON THE AREA

screen.text: What fraction of cylinders FAIL the 4,000 psi specification?

screen.mono: 28-day cylinder strength

rounds.why: Same curve, same line, other half. This is the ninety five percent answer, and handing it in when the question said "fail" is the single most common way to lose this problem.

screen.overline: PUT A FINGER ON THE AREA

screen.text: What fraction PASS the specification?

screen.mono: the same cylinders

rounds.why: Longer than means to the right, and the right tail has its own column in the table. R of z, no flip needed.

screen.overline: PUT A FINGER ON THE AREA

screen.text: What fraction of cycles run LONGER than 40 seconds?

screen.mono: signal green time

rounds.why: Two lines, one on each side, and the question wants the middle. The table has a column for exactly this: W of z is the area between minus z and plus z.

screen.overline: PUT A FINGER ON THE AREA

screen.text: What fraction fall WITHIN one standard deviation of the mean?

screen.mono: asphalt lift thickness

rounds.why: Out of tolerance is BOTH tails, and they count as one answer because it is one quantity: whatever the middle does not account for. Take W away from one.

screen.overline: PUT A FINGER ON THE AREA

screen.text: What fraction fall OUTSIDE the tolerance band?

screen.mono: a tolerance band on aggregate gradation

rounds.why: The line sits BELOW the mean, so z is negative, and the answer is still the bigger piece. A negative z never means a small answer; it means the line is on the left.

screen.overline: PUT A FINGER ON THE AREA

screen.text: What fraction of days carry MORE than 20 trucks?

screen.mono: daily truck counts

build-the-binomial.title: Build the Binomial
build-the-binomial.closing: Three factors, every time: the number of arrangements, the successes, and the failures. The exponents add up to the number of trials, and the count in front is a combination, never an arrangement.

brief.title: Three factors, every time
steps: A fixed number of yes-or-no tries
Ten pours, each one either passes or fails, and none of them affects the others. Ask how likely it is that exactly three fail. That is a binomial question.
Multiply three things
How many ways the three failures could be spread across the ten tries. Times the chance of a failure, three times over. Times the chance of a pass, seven times over. Three factors, always.
The count in front is a combination
Three failures out of ten is three failures whichever three they were, so order does not matter. Use C, not P.
Two cheap checks
The two exponents must add up to the number of tries. And whichever outcome you call the success has to be the one x is counting.
spoken: ways to arrange, times p for each success, times one minus p for each failure
tries, times the chance of a success, times the chance of a failure

picture.caption: five trials, three successes. The formula is always these three factors multiplied

rounds.why: Forty five arrangements, eight passes, two failures. Dropping the count is the error the lesson names first, and it leaves an answer far too small. The arrangement P of ten and eight would count the order the eight passed in, which nobody asked about.

screen.text: Ten asphalt samples are tested. Historically 90% of samples from this plant pass the Marshall stability test.

c.v: THE CHANCE THAT EXACTLY 8 OF THE 10 PASS

rounds.why: Calling failure the success flips p and q and flips x, and it lands on the identical product as the round before. Eight passing and two failing are the same event described from either end.

screen.text: The same ten samples, from the same plant.

c.v: THE CHANCE THAT EXACTLY 2 OF THE 10 FAIL

rounds.why: A hundred and ninety ways to pick which two were weak, two under, and eighteen that held. The exponents always add up to the number of trials, which is the cheapest check there is on this formula.

screen.text: Twenty concrete cylinders are broken. Five percent of cylinders from this mix come in under the specified strength.

c.v: THE CHANCE THAT EXACTLY 2 OF THE 20 COME IN UNDER

rounds.why: Ten passes and two rejects out of twelve. The tempting wrong pair is the fifteen percent raised to ten, which would be ten welds failing in a question about ten welds passing.

screen.text: Twelve field welds are radiographed. Eighty five percent of welds by this crew pass on the first look.

c.v: THE CHANCE THAT EXACTLY 10 OF THE 12 PASS

rounds.why: All three terms are still there; two of them are just one. There is exactly one way for everything to pass, and no failures to account for, which is why this case collapses to p to the n.

screen.text: Eight samples are tested at the plant that passes 90% of what it sends.

c.v: THE CHANCE THAT ALL 8 OF THE 8 PASS

rounds.why: Three over and twelve legal. Both probabilities are on the tray with both exponents, and only one pairing has the small probability on the small count.

screen.text: Fifteen truck loads are weighed at a static scale. Twenty percent of loads on this route are over the legal limit.

c.v: THE CHANCE THAT EXACTLY 3 OF THE 15 ARE OVER

mind-the-order.title: Mind the Order
mind-the-order.closing: The mean of the squares, take away the square of the mean. In that order, every time. The other way round gives a negative variance, which is the cheapest error to spot and the easiest to make.

brief.title: The mean of the squares, less the square of the mean
steps: Two columns of scratch work
For each outcome, write its value times its chance in one column, and its value squared times its chance in the other. Total both columns.
One subtraction
The first total is the mean. Square it. Take that away from the second total. What is left is the variance.
The order is the whole trap

The mean of the squares and the square of the mean are written almost the same and are different numbers. Subtract them the wrong way round and you get a negative variance, which cannot happen. That sign is your alarm.
spoken: the mean of the squares, less the square of the mean
E(X) = \sum x P(x), \quad E(X^2) = \sum x^2 P(x)
value times chance, and value squared times chance
second total, less the first total squared

picture.caption: two columns of scratch work, then one subtraction in the right order

ops.t: mean of the squares, less the square of the mean

rounds.why: The mean of the squares comes first, and what is taken away is the square of the mean. Handing in 2.70 is handing in the mean, and handing in 8.10 is stopping halfway.

screen.mono: trucks per minute at a toll plaza

rounds.why: An outcome of zero contributes nothing to either column and still counts in the probabilities, which is what keeps the mean below one.

screen.mono: lanes closed on a night shift

rounds.why: Eighteen and sixteen sit close enough together that swapping them looks harmless, and it is the difference between a variance of two and a variance of minus two.

screen.mono: cylinders per set that come in under strength

rounds.why: Bigger outcomes make every total bigger and change nothing about the order. Four hundred and ninety take four hundred and forty one is forty nine, and the size of the numbers is not the difficulty.

screen.mono: delay in minutes at a work zone

rounds.why: Two outcomes, equally likely. The unweighted sum of squares is on the board and it is twenty six, which is not thirteen; the probabilities belong in both columns, not just the first.

screen.mono: a two-way outcome on a repair decision

rounds.why: A tight distribution has a small variance, and the two totals in the formula are nearly equal because of it. Nearly equal is exactly when the order stops being obvious.

screen.mono: crews available on a given morning

read-the-line.title: Read It Off the Line
read-the-line.closing: Median, mode and range are places on the line and can be read without adding anything up. The mean cannot, which is the difference that matters when one reading is a long way out.

brief.title: Three ways to say where the middle is
steps: Line them up
Take some readings and stack them over their values, smallest on the left. Most of the picture is right there.
The median is a position

Count in from both ends until you meet in the middle. That reading is the median. With an even count, average the middle two. One far-off reading cannot move it, because it is still just the middle one.
The mean is a total
Add every reading and divide by how many there are. A reading far out to one side drags the mean toward it, because it is in the total.
The mode is the tallest stack
Whatever value shows up most often. A set can have no mode, or more than one. On tidy data all three agree; one wild reading splits them.
spoken: add them all up, divide by the count
the one in the middle of the line

picture.caption: seven readings. The middle one sits at 13; the far one drags the mean out to 15

rounds.why: Five readings sorted, so the median is the third one along. It is a position, not a sum, which is why you can point at it without adding anything up.

screen.text: Tap the median.

screen.mono: five moisture readings, in percent

rounds.why: The mode is the tallest stack and nothing else. A set can have no mode at all, or several, which is why it is the least useful of the three centers and the easiest to read.

screen.text: Tap the value that appears most often.

screen.mono: seven blow counts

rounds.why: With an even count there is no middle reading, so the median is the average of the middle two. That average is 42.5, which is not a reading anybody took.

screen.text: Six readings. Tap the two the median sits between.

screen.mono: six cylinder strengths, in hundreds of psi

rounds.why: Range is the largest take the smallest, so it only ever looks at the two ends. Everything in between could move anywhere and the range would not change, which is why it is a poor measure of spread.

screen.text: Tap the two readings the range is measured between.

screen.mono: six cylinder strengths, in hundreds of psi

rounds.why: The median does not care how far out the stray reading is, only that it is on that side. The MEAN would be dragged up to about 14.1, well past the middle of the pack, and that gap is the whole reason both summaries exist.

screen.text: One reading is a long way out. Tap the median anyway.

screen.mono: seven traffic counts, in hundreds

rounds.why: Two values tie for the most common, so the set has two modes and neither one is more the mode than the other. A summary that can answer twice is not a summary you build a design on.

screen.text: Tap every mode.

screen.mono: eight lift thicknesses, in inches

what-weights.title: What Gets Weighted
what-weights.closing: The formula never changes. What changes is which column is the thing being averaged and which is how much each row counts for, and getting that backwards runs the arithmetic perfectly to the wrong answer.

brief.title: Some readings count for more
steps: Not every row is equal
Three batches of concrete were tested. One batch had two cylinders, one had four, one had ten. Averaging the three batch strengths as if they were equal lets two cylinders speak as loudly as ten.
Give each reading a weight
Multiply each strength by how many cylinders stood behind it, add those up, and divide by the total number of cylinders. The big batch now pulls the answer toward itself, as it should.
Name the two roles first

What is being averaged goes in as x. How much each row gets to say goes in as the weight: how long a count ran, how many were tested, how thick a layer is. Swap them and the arithmetic runs perfectly to the wrong answer.
spoken: each value times its weight, added, over the weights added

picture.caption: three batches, strength in MPa. The wide one had ten cylinders, so it pulls the average toward it

rounds.why: The question asks for an hourly volume, so the values are the hourly rates and the weights are how long each count ran. Averaging the raw vehicle counts instead answers a different question, and averaging the rates without weighting treats two hours as if they were five.

screen.text: What is the weighted average hourly traffic volume?

screen.mono: Tap the column being averaged, then the one that weights it.

rounds.why: Strength is what is being averaged and the cylinder count is how much each batch gets to say. Batch B was tested three times as often as C, so it pulls the average three times as hard.

screen.text: What is the average compressive strength across the whole pour?

screen.mono: Tap the column being averaged, then the one that weights it.

rounds.why: Thicker layers count for more, so thickness is the weight. This is the same shape as the traffic problem with the words changed, which is the point: the formula never changes, only which column plays which part.

screen.text: What is the average unit weight of the soil profile?

screen.mono: Tap the column being averaged, then the one that weights it.

rounds.why: Five weekdays against one Saturday, so the weekday figure carries five times the weight. Averaging the three numbers evenly would give the weekend two sevenths of the week and call it three.

screen.text: What is the average daily flow over the week?

screen.mono: Tap the column being averaged, then the one that weights it.

rounds.why: The roles are the same as ever, and here the weights happen to be equal, so the weighted average comes out identical to the plain one. Equal weights are the case where the extra machinery buys you nothing, and spotting that saves time.

screen.text: Every borehole was sampled the same number of times. What is the average blow count?

screen.mono: Tap the column being averaged, then the one that weights it.

rounds.why: The columns are the other way round this time. Cost is what is being averaged and volume is how much of the job each price applied to, so reading position rather than meaning gets this one backwards.

screen.text: What is the average cost per cubic yard across the whole job?

screen.mono: Tap the column being averaged, then the one that weights it.

which-readout.title: Which Line Do You Read
which-readout.closing: Sx divides by n minus one and σx divides by n, and which you want is decided by whether the readings are a sample or everything there is. Variance and the coefficient of variation are not on the screen at all.

brief.title: Sample or population, and the square root
steps: How spread out are they
Two sets can have the same middle and look nothing alike, one bunched tight and one scattered wide. The variance measures that: the average squared distance from the mean.
Back to real units
Squaring turns meters into square meters. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so it is back in the units of the data. That is the number people quote.
Divide by n minus one

If your readings are a sample of something bigger, which on this exam they almost always are, divide by one less than the count. That is Sx on the calculator. Sigma x, two lines down, divides by n and is for a whole population.
Comparing spreads in different units
Divide the standard deviation by the mean. That ratio has no units, so a spread in psi can be compared with a spread in days.
spoken: the squared gaps from the mean, added, over n minus one
the same, over the whole count
the spread as a share of the mean

picture.caption: the calculator gives both. Sx divides by n minus one and is the one the exam wants

options: It is not on this screen
rounds.why: The mean is its own line. The 64.5 beside it is the readings added up, which is the number people hand in when they stop one step early.

screen.text: Five moisture readings are in. The report wants the average moisture content.

child.v: It is not on this screen

options: It is not on this screen
